core.text: Latin often says *I have* as 'to me there is'. That is **the dative of possession (the 'to me there is' way of saying 'I have')**: the owner sits in the dative (the 'to/for' form), the thing owned is the subject, and the verb is *est* or *sunt*. *Mārcō ūna soror est* — to Marcus there is one sister: Marcus has one sister. Latin name: datīvus possessīvus.
English keeps a trace of this with things: *there is a bad smell to the room* means the room has a bad smell. Latin extends it to everyone: *mihi est* — there is to me — I have.
Owner in the dative + est / sunt + the thing owned in the nominative (the plain naming form) = 'X has Y'.

Both say who owns something. The genitive (the 'of' form) hangs on a noun: *soror Mārcī* — Marcus's sister. The dative goes with *est* and makes a whole sentence: *Mārcō est soror* — Marcus has a sister. Look at what the owner's word is attached to: a noun (genitive, *mātris*) or *est* (dative, *mātrī*).

teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Tap the word that says who has something in each sentence. What do the two words have in common?

teach.say: Latin has *habeō*, I have, but it very often says the same thing another way round: 'to me there is a dog' for 'I have a dog'. That is **the dative of possession (the 'to me there is' way of saying 'I have')**. The owner goes into the dative (the 'to/for' form) and the verb is simply *est* or *sunt*.

check.ask: Which word says who has the rose?

teach.title: Who owns, and what is owned
teach.say: Two jobs, two cases. The owner is the dative word. The thing owned is the subject, in the nominative (the subject form) — and the verb agrees with *it*, not with the owner: *Iūliō servī multī sunt*, Julius has many slaves, has *sunt* because the slaves are plural.

check.ask: Which word is the owner and which is the thing owned — and which of them does *est* agree with?

teach.title: The owner's ending on a noun
teach.say: One cell. A 2nd-declension owner takes the dative singular *-ō*: *dominō*, *amīcō*, *Iūliō*. A 1st-declension owner takes *-ae* (*Iūliae*) and a 3rd-declension one takes *-ī* (*patrī*, *mīlitī*).

check.ask: ___ meō equus albus est. My friend has a white horse. (amīcus)

teach.title: The person-words: mihi, tibi, eī
teach.say: The owner is often not a noun but a person: *mihi* (to me), *tibi* (to you), *eī* (to him, to her). These are the datives of *ego*, *tū* and *is*, and *mihi est* is the ordinary Latin for 'I have'. With a name, Latin says *Fīliō nōmen Mārcus est* — the boy has the name Marcus.

check.ask: ___ gladius est, mihi hasta est. Which word makes it 'you have'? (tū)

teach.title: Telling it from the dative of the indirect object
teach.say: Both put the person in the dative, so look at the verb. With *est* or *sunt* the dative owns: *Mārcō canis est*, Marcus has a dog. With a verb of giving, saying or showing the dative receives: *Iūlius Quīntō pirum dat*, Julius gives Quintus a pear. Same case, two jobs, and the verb decides.

check.ask: *Medicō* and *servō* are both dative. Which one has something, and which one is given something?

teach.title: Telling it from the genitive owner, and using it
teach.say: The genitive (the 'of' form) also says who owns, but it hangs on a noun: *gladius mīlitis*, the soldier's sword. The dative hangs on *est* and makes a whole sentence: *mīlitī scūtum est*, the soldier has a shield. Ask what the owner's word is attached to.

check.ask: Canis pāstōris niger est; ___ ovēs sunt. The second half has to say the shepherd *has* sheep. (pāstor)

more.text: The commonest case is a name: *Mātrī 'Aemilia' nōmen est* — the mother's name is Aemilia. With *nōmen est* the name usually stays in the nominative (*Eī nōmen est Lūcius*), but it may agree with the owner's dative (*Puerō nōmen est Mārcō*); both are correct. The relative pronoun does the same job: *Iānus est deus* — a god *cui duae faciēs sunt*, who has two faces.

The learner's notes (week 12): the dative noun is the possessor and the nominative the thing possessed (*virō est gladius* — to the man there is a sword; *fēminīs sunt pānēs*); English does something like it only for qualities (*there is a strange look to his face*); and it is common inside a relative clause with a dative relative pronoun: *ecce vir cui gladius est* — see the man who has a sword.

Ørberg brings it in with the family's names in chapter XII (*Iūliae duo frātrēs sunt*; a Roman man has *tria nōmina*). A&G §373: the dative of possession stresses the fact of owning, the genitive the owner; *mihi est* is the plain way to say *I have* when *habeō* would put too much weight on the having.
